top_evidence.document_title: Efficacy of prescribed opioids for acute pain after being discharged from the emergency department: A systematic review and meta-­ analysis
top_evidence.text: This systematic review and meta-­ analysis was prospectively registered (PROSPERO CRD42022332009). Its results are presented as per the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-­ Analysis (PRISMA) guidelines (Data S1). 29 We also followed et al . the synthesis without meta-­ analysis reporting guidelines to complement the PRISMA guidelines. 30

top_evidence.document_title: Efficacy of prescribed opioids for acute pain after being discharged from the emergency department: A systematic review and meta-­ analysis
top_evidence.text: Identified references from all databases were transferred to Covidence systematic review manager (Covidence systematic review software, Veritas Health Innovation, available at www.covid ence.org). Eight reviewers (RD, JP, MM, DW, GF, AF, AO, and AC) participated in a two-­ stage selection process of eligible studies. After duplicate removal, each citation was screened by two independent reviewers using the title and abstract for potential relevance. The full text of the remaining citations was then independently evaluated by two reviewers against inclusion and exclusion criteria. During both stages, a third reviewer (RD or AC) resolved discrepancies.

top_evidence.document_title: Efficacy of prescribed opioids for acute pain after being discharged from the emergency department: A systematic review and meta-­ analysis
top_evidence.text: Risk of bias was assessed using the Effective Practice and Organization of Care (EPOC) risk-­ of-­ bias tool. 31 Two reviewers (JP and MM) assessed the risk of bias independently, with conflicts resolved through discussion or involvement of a third reviewer (RD). RCTs were ranked as having low risk, being unclear, or having high risk of bias across nine domains (i.e., random sequence generation, allocation concealment, similarity of baseline outcome measurements, similarity of baseline characteristics, incomplete outcome data, knowledge of the allocated interventions adequately prevented during the study, protection against contamination, selective outcome reporting, and other risk of bias) and the overall risk of bias was derived. Risk-­ of-­ bias judgments for each domain across studies were summarized using risk-­ of-­ bias graphs and summaries. Unpublished studies were considered at high risk of bias.

top_evidence.document_title: Efficacy of prescribed opioids for acute pain after being discharged from the emergency department: A systematic review and meta-­ analysis
top_evidence.text: In collaboration with an information specialist, we developed a search strategy based on four search themes: 'opioid,' 'pain,' 'emergency,' and 'effectiveness' (detailed search strategies are available in Supplement Methods S1 ). The following databases were searched from their inception to May 5, 2022: CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, and PsycINFO. An updated search was performed at the end of the process during the third week of January 2023 to collect recently published papers. We also searched Clini calTr ials.gov and the International Standard Randomized Controlled Trial Number registry for ongoing studies. Gray literature was searched using Google Scholar and the first 300 hits were screened to identify any relevant studies. References from studies meeting inclusion criteria were examined and their authors were contacted to identify additional relevant studies.

top_evidence.document_title: Efficacy of prescribed opioids for acute pain after being discharged from the emergency department: A systematic review and meta-­ analysis
top_evidence.text: Data were extracted independently by two reviewers (JP and MM) using a standardized electronic sheet, and the conflicts were | resolved by consensus. Study authors were contacted when outcomes were incomplete or when ED patients were mixed in with other populations. Sample size, age range, inclusion/exclusion criteria, type of opioid, type of nonopioid analgesic, outcomes, and primary and secondary results were extracted.

top_evidence.document_title: Efficacy of prescribed opioids for acute pain after being discharged from the emergency department: A systematic review and meta-­ analysis
top_evidence.text: Our review is limited by the study population's heterogeneity (pediatric and adult), medications type/dosage, and follow-­ up duration. However, analyses were done using a random-­ effect | model, which partially compensated for this diversity and after excluding codeine, the heterogeneity was very low ( I 2 = 0%). Furthermore, results were consistent in sensitivity analyses on the adult population and in which the study with high risk of bias and the one with only placebo as a comparison was excluded. Also, we studied only opioid use after ED discharge; results could be different in another context. Most studies utilized extensive exclusion criteria and included only patients with musculoskeletal injuries in a North American population, which limit their external validity. The adult studies included only painful syndromes of sprains and strains, and none had fractures that might have been better relieved by opioids. Most included studies (five of six) used a combination of acetaminophen (one also added an NSAID) and opioid (two of them at higher acetaminophen doses than what is currently permitted) instead of opioid alone, which may have contributed to opioid efficacy. Finally, included studies were not designed to assess the risk of overdose, opioid use disorder, or long-­ term harms.

top_evidence.document_title: Efficacy of prescribed opioids for acute pain after being discharged from the emergency department: A systematic review and meta-­ analysis
top_evidence.section: Results > Search Results And Study Characteristics
top_evidence.text: The initial search strategy generated 5942 references after duplicate removal. Of these, 47 were kept for full-­ text review and seven studies were retained. One of them 36 was further removed since it used dextropropoxyphene, an opioid that has been withdrawn from the market in 2009 because of its association with lethal events. Therefore, six studies 37-­ 42 were finally included in this systematic review and meta-­ analysis (Figure 1 ). One study 39 compared two types of opioids (oxycodone and tramadol) to a placebo. Patients could consume rescue medications and placebo has demonstrated analgesic effects 43,44 ; we kept only the oxycodone versus placebo comparison as tramadol has nonopioid analgesic effects. 45 Another study 42 compared oxycodone to two nonopioids (NSAID and cyclobenzaprine); we kept only the oxycodone versus NSAIDs comparison since cyclobenzaprine is mainly a muscle relaxant. 46 One conflict on data extraction for the outcome measured in the study by Drendel et al. 40 was settled through consensus. Four differences in risk of bias assessment were observed between the two raters, two in the protection against contamination and two in the selective outcome reporting domain. These were resolved through consensus by the two raters. Four included studies 37,39,40,42 were conducted in the United States and two 38,41 in Canada; four studies 37-­ 39,42 included adult and two others 40,41 included pediatric populations (Table 1 ). All studies included patients with musculoskeletal pain; five of them 37,38,40-­ 42 had NSAIDs as a comparator and one had a placebo. 39 Three studies 37,38,40 used codeine as the opioid, and the three others used hydrocodone, 39 morphine, 41 or oxycodone. 42 Except for morphine, opioids were combined with acetaminophen and their dosage and administration frequency were not equivalent. The type of NSAIDs used also varied across studies: diflunisal, ketorolac, ibuprofen (two studies), and naproxen. Follow-­ up duration varied from 1 to 7 days and outcomes were pain relief for five studies 37-­ 39,41,42 and treatment failure (use of rescue medication) for the other. 40 The majority of studies applied extensive exclusion criteria (Supplement Table S2 ).
